scribe_response.text: Tell me about a friend from when you were young. My closest friend as a boy was Gopalan, whom everybody called Gopi, and he lived three houses down our lane. His father repaired bicycles in a tiny shed at the corner, and the shed smelled of rubber and oil. Gopi um could mend a punctured tube faster than any grown man. He was only nine. I admired that more than I admired anything my schoolbooks taught me. We were quite um different. He was loud and quick while I was quiet and careful. Somehow the um two of us fitted together like a nut and a bolt. In the afternoons we uh sat in the shed, and he showed me how a freewheel clicked and why a chain needed oil. I um would take the little ratchet apart on a newspaper and put it back together, spring by spring. Gopi's father pretended not to notice, although he always left the smallest spanner within my reach. Our great project, in the summer I turned eleven, was a water wheel in the stream behind the paddy fields. We cut the paddles from coconut husk and fixed them to a hub made from an um old bicycle wheel. What happened next? For three days it refused to turn, and Gopi wanted to give up and go fishing. I insisted that the paddles were too shallow, so we deepened them with a borrowed knife. Then the wheel began to turn, slowly at first, and we both shouted until the egrets flew off. We had no idea what to do with it, so we simply sat on the bank and watched it spin. That was enough for us, and it remains one of the happiest afternoons of my childhood. Gopi was not a good student, and the teachers often rapped his knuckles with a ruler. I tried to help him with arithmetic, but he learned better with his hands than with numbers. When I wrote out a sum, he would shake his head and ask me to, to show him with pebbles. So we spread pebbles on the um verandah floor and added them up in heaps. His mother brought us sweet banana fritters while we worked, and she called me the little professor. When we were thirteen, Gopi left school to work full time with his father. I felt his absence in the classroom like a missing tooth. Still, we met every Sunday at the stream, and he told me about the bicycles of the whole district. He knew which families had Raleighs, which had Hercules machines, and who rode too heavily uh on the pedals. Can you tell me more about that? When I went away to the engineering college, he gave me a small brass bell for my bicycle. I kept that bell on my desk for years, even after I no longer owned a, a bicycle. Later um he expanded the shed into a proper shop with three mechanics and a signboard in red paint. I visited him whenever I returned to Kerala, and we always drank tea on the same wooden bench. He had grown stout and grey, and he laughed exactly as he had at nine years old. We talked about the wheel in the stream more than anything else. He once told me that he still looked at running water and thought of our paddles. I confess that I do the same, even in a desert country where water is precious. Gopi died a few years ago, um and his son sent me a photograph of the shop with the old bench. I have it framed um beside my chessboard now. Some friendships are made of long conversations, but ours was made of tools and small repairs. I think that is why it lasted so well. Whenever something breaks in my house, I hear his voice telling me to be patient. He uh taught me that most machines forgive you if you are gentle and curious.
